Theological Virtues
thee-oh-LOJ-ih-kul VUR-chooz
noun phrase (faith, hope, and charity)
A traditional name for the three graces of 1 Corinthians 13:13 — faith, hope, and charity (love); “theological” because they have God for their object and are wrought by His grace.

📖 Biblical Definition

The theological virtues are faith, hope, and charity (love)—the three abiding graces the apostle names together: “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.” They are called theological because they have God Himself for their object and source: faith lays hold of God's truth and His Christ; hope rests on God's promise of glory; love embraces God and, for His sake, the neighbour. They are not natural attainments but graces wrought by the Spirit, distinguished in the older theology from the “cardinal” or natural virtues (prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude). Paul joins the three repeatedly: the Thessalonians' work of faith, labour of love, and patience of hope; the believer's breastplate of faith and love and helmet of the hope of salvation. The dictionary receives the triad as a true and useful summary of the Christian graces, while correcting the Roman framework in which it has often been set. Rome treats the theological virtues as infused habits that, cooperating with works, contribute to a justification by inherent righteousness. The dictionary holds rather that faith is the instrument by which the sinner is justified—receiving Christ's imputed righteousness, not its own—and that hope and love are the fruits and companions of that justifying faith, not co-causes of acceptance with God. So understood, the three abide: faith and hope have their use in this life of pilgrimage and pass into sight and possession in glory, but love abides for ever and is the greatest, for God is love, and the redeemed shall love Him perfectly when faith is sight and hope is fulfilled.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Faith, hope, and charity—the three abiding graces (1 Corinthians 13:13), called “theological” because they have God for their object and source; received as a true summary, with faith as the justifying instrument and love the greatest, against the Roman infused-merit framework.

THEOLOGICAL VIRTUES, noun phrase. Faith, hope, and charity (love), the three abiding Christian graces.

“Now abideth faith, hope, charity… the greatest of these is charity” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

Called “theological” because they have God for their object and source.

Joined by Paul: work of faith, labour of love, patience of hope (1 Thessalonians 1:3).

Faith justifies as instrument; hope and love are its fruits, not co-causes of acceptance.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Co 13:13 — "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."

1 Th 1:3 — "Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God and our Father;"

Col 1:4 — "Since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, and of the love which ye have to all the saints,"

1 Th 5:8 — "But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Rome treats the theological virtues as infused habits that, with works, contribute to a justification by inherent righteousness; the dictionary holds faith the instrument of justification and hope and love its fruits, not co-causes.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary receives the triad of faith, hope, and charity as a true and useful summary of the Christian graces, which have God for their object and are wrought by His Spirit. The correction needed is doctrinal, against the Roman framework in which the triad has often been set. Rome treats the theological virtues as infused habits that, cooperating with the believer's works, contribute to a justification grounded in inherent righteousness—so that “faith formed by love” justifies by what it does. This confounds justification with sanctification and overthrows the gospel of grace.

The dictionary holds the Reformation distinction. Faith justifies not as a virtue that merits, but as the empty hand that receives Christ's imputed righteousness; the sinner is accepted for Christ's righteousness, not his own faith, hope, or love. Hope and love are the inseparable fruits and companions of justifying faith—real, necessary, and abiding—but not co-causes of acceptance with God. So the three abide: faith passes into sight and hope into possession when the pilgrim reaches glory, but love abides for ever and is the greatest, for God is love, and the redeemed shall love Him perfectly when faith is sight and hope fulfilled.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the three graces of 1 Corinthians 13:13: pistis (faith), elpis (hope), agape (charity, love); “theological” because directed to and given by God.

expand to see more

Pistis, Greek, faith, the hand that receives Christ.

Elpis, Greek, hope, the confident expectation of promised glory.

Agape, Greek, love or charity, the greatest and abiding grace.

“Theological” virtues, having God for object and source, against the “cardinal” natural virtues.

Joined repeatedly by Paul (1 Thessalonians 1:3; 5:8; Colossians 1:4-5).

Usage

"The teacher named faith, hope, and charity the theological virtues, having God for their object."

"He held faith to justify as instrument, with hope and love its fruits, against the Roman scheme."

"She rested in the greatest, love, which abides when faith is sight and hope fulfilled."
